fields.Text: Core functional requirements for a ride-hailing system: {{c1::riders request rides}}, {{c2::drivers accept or reject rides}}, {{c3::real-time location tracking}}, and {{c4::fare calculation}}.
Key non-functional requirements: {{c1::low latency matching}} (seconds, not minutes), {{c2::high availability}}, and {{c3::strong consistency for billing/payments}} (must be accurate).
A driver location record typically includes {{c1::driverId}}, {{c2::latitude/longitude}}, {{c3::timestamp}}, and {{c4::status (available/en route/offline)}}.

Core components of a ride-hailing architecture: {{c1::location ingestion service}}, {{c2::geospatial index}}, {{c3::matching service}}, {{c4::trip/fare service}}, and {{c5::notification service}} to alert driver/rider.

A QuadTree recursively divides a 2D map into {{c1::four quadrants}}, subdividing further only in {{c2::densely populated}} areas, so each leaf node holds roughly {{c3::a small, bounded number}} of drivers.

fields.Front: Why does driver-rider matching favor low latency over strict global optimality?
fields.Back: Riders expect a match within seconds; computing a globally optimal assignment across all drivers and riders would be too slow, so systems use fast local/greedy matching within a geographic cell instead.

fields.Front: If a ride-hailing app has 5M daily active riders each requesting about 0.5 rides/day, what is the approximate ride-request QPS?
fields.Back: 5M x 0.5 / 86,400 ≈ 29 QPS on average (much higher and spikier during rush hour).

fields.Front: If 3M active drivers each send a location update every 4 seconds, what is the approximate location-update QPS?
fields.Back: 3M / 4 ≈ 750,000 updates/sec, the dominant write load in the system.

fields.Front: Why is location-update traffic, not ride requests, usually the primary scaling bottleneck in ride-hailing systems?
fields.Back: Every active driver streams a GPS ping every few seconds continuously, producing orders of magnitude more writes than the comparatively rare ride-request events.

fields.Front: What API call would a driver's app make to report its current location?
What API would a rider's app call to fetch nearby available drivers?
fields.Back: GET /riders/nearby-drivers?lat=..&lng=..&radius=.. returns a list of candidate drivers for matching.

fields.Front: Why is driver location data usually stored in-memory (e.g. Redis) rather than in a traditional disk-based relational database?
fields.Back: Location changes constantly and must be read/written with very low latency for real-time matching; an in-memory store gives the required speed, and stale entries are quickly overwritten so durability matters less.

fields.Front: Why do ride-hailing systems partition the world into geographic regions run by separate services?
fields.Back: Matching only needs nearby drivers, so partitioning by geography lets each regional service handle a bounded, local dataset independently, enabling horizontal scaling.

fields.Front: What problem does a geospatial index (QuadTree/geohash) solve in ride-hailing matching?
fields.Back: It efficiently answers 'which drivers are within X km of this rider?' without scanning every driver's location, reducing a full table scan to a fast spatial range query.
An encoding that maps a (lat, lng) pair into a short base32 string where nearby locations share common string prefixes, enabling proximity search via simple string prefix matching.

fields.Front: Why does geohash have an edge-case weakness at the boundaries of grid cells?
fields.Back: Two points can be physically very close but fall into adjacent geohash cells with completely different prefixes, so a naive prefix search can miss nearby matches near cell edges; mitigated by also checking neighboring cells.

fields.Front: Why is a greedy 'nearest available driver' approach often preferred over a globally optimal assignment algorithm for matching?
fields.Back: Global optimization (e.g. the Hungarian algorithm) is computationally expensive and slow at scale; a greedy nearest-match runs in real time and is good enough since driver availability changes every few seconds anyway.

fields.Front: Why do ride-hailing systems route location updates through a message queue (e.g. Kafka) before updating the geospatial index?
fields.Back: Buffering through a queue smooths bursty write traffic and decouples ingestion rate from index update rate, letting the index consumer update asynchronously without falling behind under load.

fields.Front: What happens to a QuadTree-based geospatial index during a surge event (e.g. a concert letting out), and how is it mitigated?
fields.Back: A dense cluster of riders/drivers in one small area creates a hotspot where one leaf node or server handles disproportionate load; mitigated by dynamically re-partitioning or further subdividing hot cells, or sharding by finer geohash precision.

fields.Front: What is the tradeoff between more frequent driver location updates (e.g. every 1s) vs. less frequent (e.g. every 10s)?
fields.Back: More frequent updates give more accurate real-time matching and ETAs but multiply write load and battery/bandwidth usage on the driver's device; less frequent updates reduce load but risk stale positions.
